accroche: With the same oral exam grade, one candidate cites an author with an ease that seems to come naturally; the other has studied just as much
contenu_vulgarise:
Two candidates get the same grade on an oral exam. One cites an author, drops a reference, finds the right word with an ease that seems natural. The other has studied just as much, sometimes more, and struggles to produce the same effect. In 1979, the sociologist Pierre Bourdieu published, in the journal *Actes de la recherche en sciences sociales* (*Proceedings of Research in the Social Sciences*), a short article that names what the examiners do not measure directly: cultural capital, that set of inherited or acquired dispositions, goods, and credentials that weighs on academic success without ever appearing on the exam paper.

## Three Ways of Having Culture

Bourdieu distinguishes three states of cultural capital. The first, embodied, comes down to “durable dispositions of the organism”: an ease with words, a familiarity with certain works, acquired by immersion since childhood. Its accumulation, he writes, costs time and “cannot indeed be done by proxy”: no one can study up on a general culture on behalf of someone else, unlike financial capital, which can be passed on with a wire transfer. The second state, objectified, is that of “cultural goods, paintings, books, dictionaries, instruments, machines”: objects that carry a culture without requiring, to be owned in the legal sense, the slightest competence to understand them. The third state, institutionalized, is that of the diploma, which turns this capital into a good recognized by all, independently of the culture the person actually possesses at the moment they are evaluated.

## What This Shifts

The interest of this distinction is not only classificatory. Bourdieu directly targets the economic theories of “human capital,” which treat academic success as the product of individual effort and talent, without seeing that it also depends on the cultural capital already invested by the family, even before entering school. The diploma, he specifies in the 1986 text that takes up and develops this thesis for an English-speaking readership, makes it possible to establish “conversion rates between cultural capital and economic capital”: it fixes, on the labor market, a monetary value for a capital that, without it, would remain invisible and incomparable from one person to another. School, presented as the institution that evaluates everyone by the same criteria, thus reproduces, in a form that seems neutral, a starting gap for which it is not responsible. One might have looked for the cause of academic success in individual gift alone; the question Bourdieu has posed ever since is what a grade really evaluates when no one starts from the same place.

citation.texte: With the academic title, a certificate of cultural competence that confers on its holder a conventional, constant, and legally guaranteed value with respect to culture, a social alchemy produces a form of cultural capital that enjoys a relative autonomy with respect to the cultural capital its holder actually possesses at a given moment.
citation.source: The Forms of Capital, in J. G. Richardson (ed.), Handbook of Theory and Research for the Sociology of Education, Greenwood, 1986, pp. 241-258

carte.punch: With the same grade, one candidate seems “naturally” cultured. There is nothing natural about it
carte.idee: Bourdieu distinguishes three states of cultural capital: embodied (an ease acquired since childhood, which cannot be bought), objectified (books, paintings, instruments), and institutionalized (the diploma, recognized on the labor market). What school evaluates thus depends on a capital inherited beforehand.

quiz.question: Why does Bourdieu distinguish an “institutionalized” state of cultural capital, alongside the embodied state?
choix: Because the state has made diplomas compulsory for practicing any skilled profession
Because school has replaced the family as the main source of transmission of cultural capital
Because the diploma gives a recognized and stable value to a competence that, without it, would remain invisible and incomparable
Because diplomas cost more to obtain than books or works of art
quiz.explication: The state does not require diplomas for every profession, school does not replace the family in the initial transmission of cultural capital embodied from childhood, and the cost of production is not what distinguishes the states of cultural capital: what makes the diploma distinctive, according to Bourdieu, is that it turns a competence into a recognized, stable, and comparable value, even for those who cannot judge that competence themselves.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What characterizes cultural capital in the embodied state?
choix: Its accumulation costs time and cannot be done by proxy
It is passed on all at once, like a bank transfer
It is measured by the number of books the family owns
It is guaranteed by a title recognized on the labor market
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The embodied state comes down to the durable dispositions of the organism, an ease acquired by immersion since childhood. No one can accumulate it on behalf of another, which distinguishes it from financial capital that can be passed on with a wire transfer.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What examples does Bourdieu give of objectified cultural capital?
choix: A diploma obtained at the end of a national competitive exam
An ease with words acquired in childhood
Paintings, books, instruments, machines
A family's address book and connections
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The objectified state is that of cultural goods: paintings, books, dictionaries, instruments, machines. These objects can be owned in the legal sense without the slightest competence to understand them, which separates them from the embodied state.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which theories does Bourdieu's article directly target?
choix: Theories of the biological reproduction of academic aptitudes
Monetary theories of diploma inflation
Theories of the social contract applied to school
Theories of human capital, which see only individual effort
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Economic theories of human capital treat academic success as the product of talent and effort. Bourdieu counters them with the cultural capital already invested by the family, well before entering school.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the diploma make possible, according to the 1986 text?
choix: Measuring exactly the culture actually possessed
Establishing exchange rates between cultural capital and economic capital
Replacing family inheritance with academic success alone
Making cultural goods accessible to all students
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The academic title fixes, on the labor market, a monetary value for a capital that would otherwise remain invisible and incomparable from one person to another. It is moreover valid independently of the culture its holder possesses at the moment they are evaluated.
